Optimizing carbon capture and storage (CCS) infrastructure development
using a python tool for source-sink matching and cluster formation
Amina Togay a , Gaini Serik b , Woojin Lee a,c,*
a
  Dept. of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Nazarbayev University, Astana, 01000, Kazakhstan
b
  Dept. of Environmental Engineering and Technology, Ghent University, Ghent, Belgium
c
  Laboratory of Environmental Systems, National Laboratory Astana, Nazarbayev University, Astana, 010000, Kazakhstan




H I G H L I G H T S                                      G R A P H I C A L A B S T R A C T

• First optimized CCS hubs in Central Asia
  using MILP modeling.
• Developed a new method with full and
  partial redirection for source-sink
  matching.
• Identified 17 storage sites with 5784 Mt
  CO2 capacity.
• Found 100 km clustering minimizes
  cost, while 240–300 km balances
  emissions.
• Created an open-source Python tool for
  flexible CCS planning.




A R T I C L E I N F O                                    A B S T R A C T

Keywords:                                                The large-scale deployment of Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) infrastructure is critical for Kazakhstan’s
Net-zero                                                 decarbonization strategy, particularly in hard-to-abate industries. This study develops an optimization-driven
Mixed integer linear programming                         framework for CCS infrastructure planning, focusing on source-sink matching and cost-effective clustering of
Multi-objective optimization
                                                         emitters. A Python-based mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model is applied to identify optimal CCS hub
CCS hubs
                                                         configurations by minimizing the total cost of capture, transportation, and storage while accounting for envi­
                                                         ronmental impact. The results demonstrate that a 100 km clustering radius achieves the lowest cost scenario,
                                                         with full redirection costing approximately $23.30 billion and partial redirection $24.02 billion. However, the
                                                         CO2 net abated is highest in this scenario, with emissions reaching 140.55 MtCO2 and 142.73 MtCO2, respec­
                                                         tively. A 240–300 km clustering radius offers a more balanced trade-off, stabilizing costs at approximately
                                                         $34.57 billion while reducing emissions. The analysis also reveals that capture costs represent the greatest
                                                         portion of total CCS expenses (50.47 % at 100 km), while transportation costs increase with clustering radius,
                                                         rising from 45.61 % to 61.01 % at 180 km. Leveraging existing pipeline infrastructure significantly improves cost
